title: Threat from disease

book.spread: 9Ca Threat from disease; 9Ca Diseases (types of disease)

oak.lesson: Differences between infectious and non-infectious disease

big_idea: People live much longer than they did 180 years ago because we understand what causes disease: pathogens, missing nutrients, faulty genes, lifestyle and the body's own immune system.
goals: I can explain how hygiene, diet, immunisation and medicines have helped people live longer.
I can give examples of the five types of disease and say which ones can be passed from person to person.

keywords.meaning: a disease caused by a pathogen that can pass from person to person (communicable)
cannot be passed from person to person
a disease caused by a lack of a nutrient in the diet
a disease caused by a fault in the DNA
a disease made more likely by the way we live, e.g. smoking
a disease in which the body's own white blood cells attack it
an obvious effect of a disease, e.g. a rash
keeping things clean so pathogens do not spread
giving a vaccine to protect against a disease

misconceptions: Non-infectious diseases such as heart disease can be 'caught' from someone. Only diseases caused by pathogens can spread from person to person.
'Germs' are one kind of thing. Pathogens come from several kingdoms: bacteria, fungi, protoctists, and viruses (which are not living organisms).
A lifestyle factor means the person will certainly get the disease. A risk factor raises the chance; it does not make the disease certain. Treat these examples with care in class.
safety: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.

slides.subtitle: What makes us ill, and why do we live so much longer than people did 180 years ago?
slides.notes: Welcome to 9C, Threat from disease. This unit covers what causes disease, how the body fights it, how we treat it, and the ecology and cell biology that explain outbreaks. Today: the big picture of disease.

slides.title: Do Now: living longer
prompt: In England and Wales in the 1840s, the median age of death was 46. Today it is 83.
1. Suggest two reasons why people live longer today.
2. Name one disease caused by a microorganism.
slides.notes: Four minutes, in books. Expected reasons: clean water and sewers, better food, vaccines, medicines such as antibiotics, hospitals. A microorganism is a living thing too small to see without a microscope. Accept flu, cholera, chickenpox, malaria, Covid-19 and so on.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read each goal aloud. Point out the key words box on the worksheet. Students with the Chinese key words sheet have the same words with Chinese beside them.

slides.title: The Broad Street pump, 1854
slides.question: In one London street, hundreds of people died of cholera in a few days. Dr John Snow mapped every death. Almost all the victims drank from one water pump. What did he suspect?
slides.caption: The John Snow pub on Broadwick (Broad) Street, Soho, next to the site of the cholera pump
text: Talk to a partner: how could water make people ill?
slides.notes: Snow suspected the water carried the disease. The pump's well was next to a leaking cesspit, so sewage with cholera bacteria got into the drinking water. The handle was removed and the outbreak stopped. This is hygiene: keeping drinking water separate from sewage.

slides.title: Why do we live longer?
slides.caption: Oral polio vaccine being given to a child
text: Hygiene keeps drinking water separate from sewage, which contains pathogens (cholera, typhoid).
Better diet: healthier bodies fight disease better.
Immunisation protects against particular diseases. Polio paralysed or killed about half a million people a year in the 1940s; today there are a few hundred cases.
Medicines, including antibiotics for bacterial diseases.
slides.key_idea: Hygiene, diet, immunisation and medicines have cut deaths from infectious diseases.
slides.notes: Polio is caused by a virus that attacks the nervous system, so signals cannot reach muscles and the person cannot move. An international immunisation programme has almost wiped it out. Ask: which of these four changes could a single family do for itself, and which need a whole town?

slides.title: Five types of disease
slides.text: A disease is something that makes you ill. Diseases have many different causes.
slides.key_idea: Only infectious diseases can be passed from person to person. The other four types are non-communicable.
slides.notes: Go through each row: infectious (a pathogen gets in), deficiency (a nutrient is missing), genetic (a fault in the DNA, present from birth), lifestyle (smoking, poor diet, too little exercise raise the risk), autoimmune (the immune system attacks the body, e.g. type 1 diabetes). Ask students to name one more example for the first two rows.

slides.title: Pathogens and symptoms
text: Pathogens are microorganisms that get into the body and change how it works.
They include bacteria, fungi, protoctists and viruses.
The obvious effects of a disease are its symptoms: a rash, a raised temperature, a cough.
In richer countries, most deaths are now from changes inside the body, not from infections.
slides.key_idea: A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease.
slides.notes: Bacteria, fungi and protoctists are three kingdoms of living organisms. Viruses are not classed as living: they cannot do anything on their own and must get inside a cell to copy themselves. Chickenpox is a virus; athlete's foot is a fungus; malaria is a protoctist carried by mosquitoes; cholera is a bacterium.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.instruction: Mini whiteboards. One answer each, then we check.
questions: Scurvy is caused by too little vitamin C. Which type of disease is it?
Flu is caused by a virus. Which type of disease is it?
Can you catch type 1 diabetes from a friend? Yes or no.
Name one kingdom of organisms that includes pathogens.
slides.notes: Answers: deficiency; infectious (communicable); no, it is autoimmune and non-communicable; bacteria, fungi or protoctists (viruses are not a kingdom of living things); a rash or spots, itching, a raised temperature.

slides.title: Your turn: sorting diseases
steps: Core: match each type of disease to its example, then tick communicable or non-communicable.
Core: fill the gaps using the word bank; decide what type of disease anaemia is.
Stretch: write definitions; explain why polio stops muscles working.
Challenge: why are most deaths in richer countries now non-communicable? How do medicines get into cells?
Finished? Answer the My thinking question.
slides.footer: Use the key words box. Write the type of disease, not just the name of the disease.
slides.notes: The match question has one example for each type. Common error: calling cardiovascular disease infectious because it is common. Circulate and ask students to say the cause of each disease out loud.

slides.title: A changing threat
slides.prompt: In richer countries, the main causes of death are now non-communicable diseases such as heart disease and cancer, not infections. Why has this changed over the last 180 years?
frames: Fewer people die from infections because ___.
More people now die from ___ because they live long enough to ___.
One thing we could do about lifestyle diseases is ___.
slides.notes: Expected: hygiene, vaccines and antibiotics have cut deaths from infectious diseases, so people live longer, and diseases of older age (heart disease, cancer) become the main causes of death; lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, exercise) also matter. Keep the discussion factual and avoid singling out anyone's family habits.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: Give one example of a non-communicable disease and explain why it is non-communicable.
Name two types of microorganism that can be pathogens.
slides.notes: Answers: a microorganism that causes disease; e.g. scurvy (lack of vitamin C) or sickle cell disease (faulty gene) or type 1 diabetes (immune system attacks the body): none is caused by a pathogen, so it cannot pass from person to person; bacteria, viruses, fungi, protoctists. Collect the strips before students leave.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Immunity and vaccination: how white blood cells destroy pathogens, and why you only get measles once.
points: People live longer because of hygiene, better diet, immunisation and medicines.
Pathogens are microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protoctists) that cause infectious diseases.
Deficiency, genetic, lifestyle and autoimmune diseases are non-communicable: they cannot be passed on.
Symptoms are the obvious effects of a disease.
slides.notes: Homework: Workbook pages 27 and 28 (9Ca Threat from disease; Diseases). Students with the Chinese key words sheet may answer in either language but should use the English key words.

stretch.q: Define each word in one sentence.
The polio virus damages nerves that carry signals to muscles. Explain why this can stop a person moving their legs.
The text says polio affected 'an estimated half a million people' a year. Explain what 'estimated' means here and why an exact number was not possible.

challenge.q: In richer countries, most deaths are now caused by non-communicable diseases rather than by infections. Explain why this has changed since the 1840s. Use the words hygiene, immunisation and lifestyle in your answer.
Medicines taken by mouth are absorbed into the blood and then enter cells by diffusion. Explain how diffusion happens, using ideas about particles.

worksheet.my_thinking: Which has saved more lives: clean water or medicines? What information would you need to decide?
exit: Give one example of a non-communicable disease and explain why it is non-communicable.
Name two types of microorganism that can be pathogens.

core: deficiency: scurvy; infectious: flu; lifestyle: lung cancer linked to smoking; genetic: sickle cell disease; autoimmune: type 1 diabetes.
Communicable: cholera, chickenpox, malaria. Non-communicable: anaemia, cardiovascular disease, haemophilia.
stretch: Pathogen: a microorganism that causes disease. Hygiene: keeping things clean (e.g. drinking water separate from sewage) so pathogens do not spread. Immunisation: giving a vaccine so the body becomes protected (immune) against a particular disease.

Secure answer: muscles only contract when they receive electrical impulses along nerves from the brain and spinal cord. If the virus damages those nerves, the impulses cannot reach the leg muscles, so the muscles do not contract and the person cannot move their legs (paralysis).

Estimated means the number is an approximate calculation, not an exact count. It was not possible to count every case because many countries did not record every patient, some people were never diagnosed, and data from many areas could not be collected.
challenge: Secure answer: in the 1840s many people died young from infectious diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Hygiene (clean water, sewers), immunisation (vaccines against polio, measles and so on) and antibiotics mean that far fewer people now die from infections. People therefore live much longer, and diseases that develop inside the body over a lifetime, such as heart disease and cancer, become the main causes of death. Lifestyle factors (smoking, unhealthy diet, too little exercise) increase the risk of these non-communicable diseases.

Secure answer: the medicine dissolves, so its particles are moving randomly all the time. There are more medicine particles in the blood than inside the cells, so there is a concentration gradient. More particles move from the blood (higher concentration) into the cells (lower concentration) than move the other way, so overall the medicine spreads into the cells. Diffusion does not need energy from the cell.
exit: e.g. scurvy (caused by a lack of vitamin C), sickle cell disease (a faulty gene) or type 1 diabetes (the immune system attacks the pancreas): it is not caused by a pathogen, so it cannot be passed from person to person.
Any two of: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protoctists.
answers.my_thinking: Open answer. A good answer names the information needed: numbers of deaths from water-borne diseases before and after clean water supplies, numbers of deaths prevented by antibiotics and vaccines, and the dates when each change happened in different countries. Historians generally credit clean water and sewers with the biggest early fall in deaths.
